t: Password Strength — Count Distinct Characters by Class
o: We must score a password based on **distinct** characters only: each distinct lowercase letter adds 1, each distinct uppercase letter 2, each distinct digit 3, and each distinct special character from "!@#$" adds 5. Duplicates contribute nothing extra. In Example 1, "aA1!" has four distinct characters spanning all four classes, giving 1+2+3+5 = 11. In Example 2, "bbB11#" has duplicates ('b' twice, '1' twice), but the distinct set is {b, B, 1, #}, again scoring 1+2+3+5 = 11. With length up to 10^5 and characters limited to letters, digits, and four specials, any single pass with a set or boolean flags is easily fast enough.
k: Only the *set* of distinct characters matters — deduplicate before scoring.
Character class determines the score: lowercase=1, uppercase=2, digit=3, special in "!@#$"=5.
A single pass with fixed-size boolean arrays (or a hash set) achieves O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash Set of Seen Characters
a.i: Insert every character into a set; after the pass, iterate over the set and add the score for each class. This directly mirrors the problem statement and is trivially correct.
s: Create an empty set and insert every character of the password.
For each character c in the set, determine its class.
Add 1/2/3/5 to the answer depending on whether c is lowercase, uppercase, digit, or one of "!@#$".
a.t: O(n) — one pass to build the set plus at most 62+4 iterations over it.
a.sp: O(1) — the set holds at most 62 distinct characters regardless of input size.

a.i: Since the alphabet is tiny and known, use three counters (or boolean arrays) tracking which lowercase, uppercase, digit, and special characters have appeared. Score is then computed from counts without storing a general-purpose set — slightly faster constant factors and no hashing overhead.
s: Initialize four boolean arrays (size 26, 26, 10, 4) or equivalent counters to false.
Scan the password once; mark the flag corresponding to each character's class and index.
Count marked entries in each array as cntLower, cntUpper, cntDigit, cntSpecial.
a.t: O(n) — one linear scan over the password plus constant-size bookkeeping.
a.sp: O(1) — fixed-size boolean arrays independent of input length.

w: In an interview, lead with the hash-set approach since it directly encodes the statement, then mention the boolean-array version as the optimal refinement. The main pitfall is forgetting that repeated characters count once — always deduplicate first. Edge cases: a single-character string scores its class value alone; a string of one repeated character also scores just that class's value. Maximum possible strength is 26·1 + 26·2 + 10·3 + 4·5 = 118. Likely follow-ups: handle Unicode or additional special sets (generalize via a score map), or compute strength of substrings efficiently (precompute prefix distinct-class counts).
